analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum daily nurse staffing hours in nursing homes and bans forced arbitration of abuse claims.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote: it sat in two House committees from November 2019 until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require Medicare and Medicaid nursing homes to provide at least 4.1 hours of nursing care per resident per day, with specific staffing ratios for each shift, and to post their daily staffing levels where residents can see them. It would also raise nurse aide training from 75 to 120 hours, protect nurses from being fired for refusing assignments that violate staffing rules, require written consent before giving residents psychotropic drugs for unapproved uses, and ban nursing homes from forcing residents or employees into pre-dispute arbitration — meaning abuse and neglect claims could go to court instead of a private arbitrator.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 1.4 million people living in Medicare and Medicaid-certified nursing homes, their families, and the nurses and aides who care for them. Residents would get guaranteed staffing levels, public posting of staffing data, consent before off-label psychotropic drugging, and the right to sue in court. Nurses and aides would gain whistleblower protections and more training.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and direct-care nurses

how_it_helps.text: Requires each Medicare and Medicaid nursing home to provide a total of at least 4.1 hours of nursing care per resident per day — 0.75 by a registered nurse, 0.54 by a licensed practical nurse, and 2.81 by a nurse aide — with specific ratios for day, evening, and night shifts.

Facilities that fall short face denial of payments for new admissions, civil money penalties of up to $10,000 per day of noncompliance, public listing of violators on a federal website, and possible termination from Medicare and Medicaid after repeated failures.
Requires facilities to post daily staffing levels at each nurses' station and make the past 12 months of staffing information available to the public on request.
Bars nursing homes from requiring pre-dispute arbitration agreements from residents or employees, and voids existing such agreements, so abuse and neglect claims can proceed in court.

Protects nurses who refuse work assignments they believe violate staffing requirements or that they are not qualified to perform safely, with reinstatement, back pay, and attorneys' fees available through federal court.

Requires written informed consent before prescribing a psychotropic drug to a resident for a use not approved by the FDA, and directs HHS to add a measure of psychotropic drug use to the Nursing Home Compare five-star rating website.

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home operators, who would have to hire substantially more nurses and aides to meet the ratios, cover higher training costs, and give up forced arbitration — a tool that keeps abuse and neglect claims out of court. Some of that cost could flow through to Medicare, Medicaid, and private-pay families if reimbursement is not raised to match.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing home operators, via hiring and legal costs

drawbacks.text: The staffing mandate would raise labor costs sharply at a time when many facilities already report difficulty recruiting nurses and aides; without a matching increase in Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement, facilities could cut elsewhere, close, or shift costs to other payers — a risk the bill itself acknowledges by ordering a study of the requirements' impact on facility reimbursement.
Raising required nurse aide training from 75 to 120 hours would shrink the pipeline of new aides in the short term, since fewer people could complete certification quickly enough to fill openings.

The bill's enforcement relies on states and the HHS Secretary identifying understaffed facilities through surveys; understaffing has historically been under-detected, so the protections could be weaker in practice than on paper.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real: guaranteed staffing clearly improves care, and the cost falls on an industry whose business model has often depended on lean staffing. The main design weakness is that the bill imposes the staffing floor without appropriating additional money to pay for it, leaving facilities to absorb the cost or pass it to public programs — but it also includes an enforcement structure, public disclosure, and whistleblower protections that go beyond the staffing numbers themselves.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees and then to a Health subcommittee, and neither committee ever took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on November 21, 2019, with 40 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors.
It was referred to both the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees on the day of introduction, and to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee the next day.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action of any kind appears in the action history through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home operators came out ahead: no staffing mandates, no public posting of daily staffing levels, no whistleblower protections, and no ban on forced arbitration ever took effect. Residents and direct-care nurses gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing home operators avoided all new mandates

sides.party_line_note: All 41 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no vote was ever taken, so the record shows Democratic support but no recorded position from any House Republican.

industries.note: The bill would force facilities to hire many more nurses and aides to hit 4.1 hours of care per resident per day, publicly post daily staffing, and face penalties up to $10,000 per day for violations. It would also void forced arbitration agreements, letting residents and employees take abuse and neglect claims to court instead of private arbitration.

industries.industry: Direct-care nursing workforce (RNs, LPNs, nurse aides)
industries.note: The bill guarantees staffing levels, raises required nurse aide training from 75 to 120 hours, and gives nurses a federally protected right to refuse unsafe assignments without retaliation, with court remedies.

By voiding pre-dispute arbitration agreements in nursing facilities and home and community-based care, the bill removes a stream of mandated arbitration business that providers currently impose on residents and employees.

The bill requires written informed consent before off-label psychotropic prescriptions and would add a utilization measure to the federal five-star rating website, which could deter casual off-label prescribing in nursing homes without banning any drug.
